'''Charlotte Friend''' (March 11, 1921 – January 13, 1987) was an American virologist. She is best known for her discovery of the [[Friend virus|Friend leukemia virus]].<ref name="pmid13416470">{{cite journal| author=FRIEND C| title=Cell-free transmission in adult Swiss mice of a disease having the character of a leukemia. | journal=J Exp Med | year= 1957 | volume= 105 | issue= 4 | pages= 307–18 | pmid=13416470 | doi= 10.1084/jem.105.4.307| pmc=2136697 }}</ref> She helped to establish the concept of the [[oncovirus]], studied the role of the host immune response in disease development, and helped define modern [[retrovirology]].

== Biography==

=== Family ===
Born and raised in New York, she was the youngest daughter of Russian Jewish immigrants, Morris Friend, a businessman, and Cecilia (Wolpin) Friend, a pharmacist. Friend had three siblings, two older sisters, Priscilla and Leafan, and a younger brother, Morris. When she was three years old, her father died, leaving her mother alone to raise four children during the Great Depression. Her mother made sure all four of her children completed their education, despite living on "Home Relief".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://jwa.org/encyclopedia/article/friend-charlotte|title=Charlotte Friend {{!}} Jewish Women's Archive|website=jwa.org|language=en|access-date=2017-07-19}}</ref>

=== Education and research ===
She graduated from Hunter High School in 1940 and Hunter College in 1944.<ref name="Icahn">{{cite web |title=Friend, Charlotte, PhD, Papers, 1935-1987 |url=https://icahn.mssm.edu/about/srt/archives/collection/charlotte-friend |website=Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai |access-date=11 May 2026}}</ref> That same year, she enlisted in the United States Navy.<ref name="JWA" /> As a lieutenant junior grade she worked in the hematology laboratory at [[U.S. Naval Hospital Shoemaker]], California.<ref name="JWA">{{cite web | url=http://jwa.org/encyclopedia/article/friend-charlotte | title=Charlotte Friend | publisher=[[Jewish Women's Archive]]| author=Diamond, Leila | accessdate=December 31, 2014}}</ref> After the war ended she enrolled as a graduate student in the Department of Microbiology at [[Yale]], where she received her PhD in 1950 with a thesis on the effects of [[sodium salicylate]] (aspirin) on antigen-antibody reactions<ref name="NAP">{{cite web | url=https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/friend-charlotte.pdf | title=Biographical Memoirs (vol.63): Charlotte Friend | publisher=[[The National Academies Press]] |year=1994| access-date=December 31, 2014 | author=Diamond, Leila}}</ref> During her time at Yale she frequently traveled to New York to consult with [[Elvin Kabat]] and [[Michael Heidelberger]], eminent immunologists at Columbia.<ref name="NAP" /> As a post-doc she worked at the [[Sloan-Kettering Institute]] under the direction of [[Cornelius P. Rhoads]]. While at Sloan-Kettering, she met Cecily Cannan Selby, who had recently earned her Ph.D. from the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. Both scientists were interested in cell structure. Once, when looking through an unused [[electron microscope]] at the university, they decided to look at fine structures within the cells of the [[Ehrlich ascites carcinoma]], a commonly used model for [[cancer research]]. What they found were structures in the cytoplasm of the cells which resembled those found in virus-infested cells. It was this incident that sparked Friend's interest in the possibility of [[cancer being caused by viruses]], which became a main focus of her research.  In 1966 she accepted a position as professor and director of the Center for Experimental Cell Biology at The [[Mount Sinai Hospital, New York|Mount Sinai Hospital]].

At various times, she was president of the [[Harvey Society]] (1978-79), the [[American Association for Cancer Research]] (1975-76) and the [[New York Academy of Sciences]] (1978), and was the first woman to do so.<ref name="Icahn" /><ref name=NAP/> In 1998, the American Association for Cancer Research established the [https://www.aacr.org/awards/aacr-women-in-cancer-research-charlotte-friend-lectureship/ AACR-Women in Cancer Research Charlotte Friend Lectureship] in her honor to recognize scientists who have made significant contributions to cancer research and advanced the role of women in science.<ref>{{Cite web |title=AACR-WR Women in Cancer Research Charlotte Friend Lectureship |url=https://www.aacr.org/awards/aacr-women-in-cancer-research-charlotte-friend-lectureship/ |access-date=January 16, 2026 |website=American Association for Cancer Research}}</ref> Charlotte Friend also served as a member of the Advisory Committee for the Virus Cancer Program of the [[National Institutes of Health]] and a member of the Board of Scientific Counselors of the Division of Cancer Cause and Prevention of the [[National Cancer Institute]]. Over the years, she served on a number of other advisory committees and on the editorial boards of several cancer and [[hematology]] journals. In all, she published 163 papers, 70 of which she wrote by herself or with one other author.

On her sixtieth birthday she was diagnosed with a [[lymphoma]]. She was insistent that her diagnosis remain secret, and continued to carry out her duties in her laboratory.<ref name=NAP/> She died in 1987 at the age of 65.

== Legacy ==
* Cemented the knowledge that virus can be responsible for some types of cancer. 
* Friend Virus is today the model to study viral leukemogenesis <ref>L. Diamond and S. R. Wolman, eds., "Viral Oncogenesis and Cell Differentiation: The Contributions of Charlotte Friend." (Ann. N.Y. Acad. Sci. 567, 1989).</ref>
* Helped set the foundations for the study of retrovirus. Her techniques and characterisation studies allowed the future isolation of the human immunodeficiency virus. 
* Observed the relation between liver cell damage and virus release and elevation of enzyme levels. Furthermore, she detected that increases in serum enzymes are also a feature of some human leukaemia, both still of vital clinical relevance today.<ref>{{cite journal | pmc = 2136542 | pmid=13271682 | volume=102 | issue=6 | title=Glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase activity of serum in mice with viral hepatitis | year=1955 | journal=J. Exp. Med. | pages=699–704 | last1 = Friend | first1 = C | last2 = Wroblewski | first2 = F | last3 = LA | first3 = DUE JS | doi=10.1084/jem.102.6.699}}</ref>
* Observed the cytodifferentiating effect of [[Dimethyl sulfoxide|DMSO]] which laid the groundwork for the development of [[Histone deacetylase inhibitor|HDAC inhibitors]]<ref>{{Citation |last=Breslow |first=Ronald |chapter=From DMSO to the Anticancer Compound SAHA, an Unusual Intellectual Pathway for Drug Design |date=2016-12-02 |chapter-url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/9783527800315.ch1 |title=Successful Drug Discovery |pages=1–11 |editor-last=Fischer |editor-first=János |place=Weinheim, Germany |publisher=Wiley-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA |language=en |doi=10.1002/9783527800315.ch1 |isbn=978-3-527-80031-5 |access-date=2022-11-18 |editor2-last=Childers |editor2-first=Wayne E.}}</ref>

== Prize and Honors==
* 1962 Alfred P. Sloan Award in Cancer Research
* 1979 [[Leopold Griffuel Prize]]
* 1979 [[U.S. National Academy of Sciences]]
* 1986 Honorary Doctor of Science, [[Brandeis University]]

== Selected works ==
*“Cell-Free Transmission in Adult Swiss Mice of a Disease Having the Character of a Leukemia.” ''[[Journal of Experimental Medicine]]'' 105 (1957): 307–318<ref name="JWA"/>
*“The Coming of Age of Tumor Virology.” ''[[Cancer Research (journal)|Cancer Research]]'' 37 (1977): 1255–1263<ref name="JWA"/>
*“Hemoglobin Synthesis in Murine Virus-induced Leukemic Cells in Vitro: Stimulation of Erythroid Differentiation by Dimethyl Sulfoxide,” with W. Scher, J.G. Holland, and T. Sato. ''[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]'' 68 (1971): 378–382.<ref name="JWA"/>
